item.content: {"url": "https://api.crossref.org/works?query=thermodynamic+constraints+and+stoichiometric+network+conditions+for+non-equilibrium+persistence+and+chemical+memory&rows=4&select=DOI%2Ctitle%2Cabstract%2CURL%2Cpublished", "scope": "Crossref bibliographic metadata and abstracts where supplied; not full papers", "excerpt": "[{\"DOI\": \"10.1007/bf03155789\", \"title\": [\"Non-equilibrium thermodynamic description of transport processes of interstitial defects in non-stoichiometric crystals under isothermal conditions\"], \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.1007/bf03155789\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[1989, 12]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.6286378\", \"title\": [\"Management Without Equilibrium Management Under Non-Equilibrium Conditions: A Persistence-Oriented Theory of Management\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p><p><span>Once the structural unavailability of long-term management equilibrium is acknowledged, management theory faces an unavoidable reorientation: if stability and optimal control cannot be achieved in principle, how should the purpose of management be coherently redefined?</span></p>\\n<p><span>&nbsp;</span><span>This paper develops a management framework that takes persistent non-equilibrium as its normal condition rather than as an anomaly. Under the constraint of the First Theorem of Organizational Instability, it argues that the core objective of management should no longer be defined as achieving or maintaining stability or optimality, but as sustaining organizational persistence under ongoing instability and uncertainty.</span></p>\\n<p><span>&nbsp;</span><span>By systematically distinguishing stability, success, and persistence—three concepts frequently conflated in management theory—the paper identifies persistence as the only management objective that remains structurally consistent under non-equilibrium conditions. On this basis, it formulates four foundational principles of management without equilibrium: abandoning long-term optimality as a governing objective, institutionalizing tolerance for fluctuation and failure, prioritizing structural redundancy over extreme efficiency, and replacing static planning with dynamic governance.</span></p>\\n<p><span>&nbsp;</span><span>The paper further examines the implicati…
